entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310 – c. 230 BCE) was a groundbreaking Hellenistic Greek astronomer and mathematician, widely recognized as the first known individual to propose a comprehensive heliocentric model of the cosmos, placing the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the universe. Active primarily in the intellectual ferment of the 3rd century BCE, an era marked by the flourishing of scientific inquiry in Alexandria and other centers, his work fundamentally challenged the geocentric paradigm dominant for millennia. Though his radical theories were largely dismissed by his contemporaries, Aristarchus's audacious vision laid the conceptual groundwork for the Copernican revolution nearly 1,800 years later, cementing his posthumous stature as a visionary ahead of his time.

His most significant extant work, *On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon*, demonstrates a sophisticated application of geometry to astronomical observation. Though based on a geocentric premise for its specific calculations, the text showcases his rigorous methodology. Crucially, it was Aristarchus who extended these geometric principles to deduce the vast distances involved, leading him to conclude that the Earth must revolve around a far larger, stationary Sun, and that the stars were immensely distant. He proposed that the Earth rotated on its axis daily and orbited the Sun annually, while the stars remained fixed. This model required a universe of immense, previously unimagined scale to explain the absence of stellar parallax, a phenomenon not observed until the 19th century.
